Unocoin says suspected misuse of backup wallet access enabled unauthorized transfers outside BitGo as the exchange investigates losses.

Crypto exchange Unocoin said on Nov. 13 that disputed wallet transfers were signed and broadcast outside BitGo, while the freeze on its BitGo enterprise account had worked so far.

It has been revealed that the exchange suspended all services on Nov. 9 after detecting further unauthorized activity. It had requested freezes on its enterprise accounts at BitGo and Fireblocks after initially detecting the activity on Nov. 6.

In its incident enhancement, Unocoin mentioned a backup mechanism designed to preserve access to funds if BitGo became unavailable appeared to have been exploited. It is still investigating how that mechanism was used, cryptocurrency losses, and potential information exposure.

In a recent development, bitGo's wallet documentation describes three keys: the user key, backup key, and BitGo key. Normal transactions use the user and BitGo keys to meet a two-of-three signing requirement. The backup key can instead pair with either of the other two keys.

Pairing the backup key with the user key provides a signing route that does not require BitGo's key, and the two-of-three requirement still applies in that recovery arrangement.

What changes is the pair of keys used to satisfy it: the user and backup keys replace the usual user-and-provider combination, leaving BitGo outside that signing process.

BitGo notes that limit in its withdrawal-policy documentation, saying that those policies apply only to transactions involving BitGo. Recovery transactions using the user and backup keys bypass the policies configured with the provider.

#6. Breaking: Could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words)
Hardware & Chips

Breaking: Could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://decrypt.co/383276/nvidia-arm-ceo-rene-haas-replace-jensen-huang

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang?
  • Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to the Financial Times, putting a former Nvidia executive in contention for one of technology's biggest jobs.
  • Haas is one of several people under consideration, people familiar with the matter told the FT.

In a recent development, could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate.

Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to the Financial Times, putting a former Nvidia executive in contention for one of technology's biggest jobs.

Haas is one of several people under consideration, people familiar with the matter told the FT. There is no guarantee he will receive an offer or accept one. The FT noted he maintains strong ties to Huang and some Nvidia directors.

According to recent reports, nvidia's board told Reuters it was still selecting an executive search firm and had not formally engaged any candidate. “Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature,” it noted.

Sources indicate that huang resigned Thursday after 33 years leading the company he co-founded, following reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a business executive suspected by U.S. officials of having Chinese intelligence ties. The company remarked it had no reason to believe its secrets were compromised.

It has been revealed that chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones has become board chair. Analysts have also floated Nvidia data-center executive Ian Buck and AMD chief Lisa Su as possible successors, though those names are not confirmed appointments or offers.

Industry observers note that an internal Nvidia suggestion-box post has attracted more than 1,600 comments, many supportive of Huang's reinstatement, according to Wired. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one anonymous employee wrote.

Other staff members have demanded transparency around his departure. The campaign highlights Huang still has supporters inside Nvidia; it does not mean the board has opened talks to reinstate him.

In a recent development, haas, 64, is a Silicon Valley-based semiconductor executive whose career spans engineering, product development and sales. He earned an electrical engineering degree from Clarkson University and worked at chip companies Tensilica and Scintera Networks before joining Nvidia in 2006.

He spent seven years at Nvidia as vice president and general manager of its computing products business, then moved to Arm in 2013. At Arm, he rose from strategic alliances to chief commercial officer in 2015 and head of its intellectual-property products group in 2017, before becoming CEO in February 2022.

That appointment came as Nvidia's proposed $40 billion takeover of Arm collapsed under pressure from regulators. Haas was suddenly running a business his former employer had tried, unsuccessfully, to buy.

In a recent development, he steered Arm back onto the Nasdaq in September 2023 at an initial valuation of about $54.5 billion, one of the year's largest stock-market debuts. The IPO also gave Japanese owner SoftBank a way to sell shares while retaining control.

Unlike Nvidia, which primarily sells graphics processors and related computing systems, Arm licenses chip designs and computing architecture to companies including Apple, Amazon and Qualcomm, earning fees and royalties when customers use its technology. Arm-based designs are now increasingly found in cloud servers as well as phones.

Arm reported $1.44 billion in revenue for the quarter ended September 30, up 27% from a year earlier. Royalties from data-center chips doubled, while Arm remarked initial commercial deliveries of its fresh CPU remain on track for early 2027.

Haas also sits on SoftBank's board and, since April, has served as CEO of SoftBank Group International, helping oversee its semiconductor and AI interests. A move to Nvidia would require untangling those ties, particularly because the companies are partners whose interests increasingly overlap in data-center hardware.

For Nvidia, the next leader would inherit not just its lead in AI chips, but delicate relationships with governments and customers as Washington debates tighter export restrictions on China. Nvidia is scheduled to report earnings on November 17, with Kress at the helm and its permanent CEO search still underway.

Industry observers note that need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.

Today in crypto, OpenAI introduced AI payments in ChatGPT, Jane Street nearly eightfold its Fidelity Bitcoin ETF holdings while trimming its BlackRock stake, and Trump nominated four SEC and CFTC commissioners, including a replacement for Hester Peirce.

OpenAI on Friday introduced a new feature allowing AI agents to make purchases on behalf of people directly within ChatGPT through existing payment networks, in collaboration with American Express, Mastercard and Visa.

The wallet lets people authorize transactions using biometric verification, such as facial recognition or fingerprints. Payment networks generate tokenized card credentials for each approved purchase, keeping users’ actual card details from merchants and AI agents, the firm said.

The launch comes as AI companies seek to move beyond product recommendations into executing transactions, potentially changing how consumers interact with online merchants. OpenAI noted it is working with payment processors and fraud prevention firms to support AI purchases through existing checkout systems.

Jane Street’s share count in Fidelity’s spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) rose nearly eightfold in the third quarter, while its holdings in BlackRock’s fund fell 19%.

Sources indicate that the trading giant ended September with 7.01 million shares of Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC0, up from about 887,000 at the end of June. The position was worth $509 million on Sept. 30, according to its second-quarter and third-quarter filings.

Industry observers note that jane Street’s holdings in BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) fell to 20.22 million shares from 24.88 million. A higher share price lifted the reported value of its stake to $957 million from $828 million.

Jane Street was the largest reported institutional holder of BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF at the end of June after boosting its share count by 324% in Q2, according to 13F Pro. IBIT is the world’s largest spot Bitcoin ETF with $56 billion in net assets as of Thursday.

The firm also added nearly 9 million shares (about $249 million) of the ARK 21Shares Bitcoin ETF (ARKB), while more than doubling its holdings in BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA) by 7.83 million shares (about $158 million).

US President Donald Trump has nominated Steven Levine to replace former Securities and Exchange Commission Commissioner Hester Peirce, one of the agency’s most prominent crypto advocates, as part of four nominations to fill vacancies at the SEC and Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

Sources indicate that the White House’s latest announcement on Thursday named two nominees each for the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, agencies whose decisions help shape US cryptocurrency regulation, among other functions. All four nominations require Senate confirmation.

The nominations would replenish several commissioner roles. The SEC currently has only two of its five commissioner seats filled, while CFTC Chairman Michael Selig is the sole member of his agency’s five-seat commission.

The nominations come weeks before Democrats are set to take control of the Senate in January, giving a narrow window for Republicans to confirm Trump’s picks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Should Government Officials Be Banned From Prediction Markets?
  • The chairman of the House Oversight Committee is raising the prospect of barring government officials from trading on prediction markets, citing concerns that insiders are using nonpublic information to profit on platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket.
  • In a staff memorandum released Friday, the committee detailed an investigation into insider trading by government officials, military personnel and people holding security clearances who have placed bets using information not available to the public.

Should Government Officials Be Banned From Prediction Markets? House Oversight Says Maybe.

The chairman of the House Oversight Committee is raising the prospect of barring government officials from trading on prediction markets, citing concerns that insiders are using nonpublic information to profit on platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket.

In a staff memorandum released Friday, the committee detailed an investigation into insider trading by government officials, military personnel and people holding security clearances who have placed bets using information not available to the public.

The probe gathered nearly 1,700 pages of documents and included five bipartisan staff briefings from prediction market platforms about how they detect and report suspicious activity.

Chairman James Comer framed the issue around public trust. “Americans are rightly concerned about public corruption,” he noted, arguing Congress “has a duty to ensure our laws adequately prevent insider trading” and prohibit officials “from profiting from nonpublic information.”.

He said lawmakers must weigh “additional reforms to prevent public corruption and restore the American people’s trust in government.”.

The memo’s central recommendation is that Congress consider new restrictions on federal personnel, ranging from an outright ban on trading prediction markets to narrower limits on specific contracts, such as those tied to government decisions.

Applying such rules across all branches, the committee argued, would reinforce that government employees shouldn’t financially benefit from access to nonpublic information, and would remove even the appearance of it.

In a recent development, the memo stressed that existing insider trading laws already apply to prediction markets. It cited the Commodity Exchange Act, as amended by the STOCK Act, which bars federal employees, members of Congress and others from trading commodity futures, options, or swaps on nonpublic information drawn from their positions.

The committee credited the platforms themselves for policing their markets, noting that most reported insider trading incidents were first detected and flagged to regulators by the platforms. It singled out Polymarket, which recently hired a former law enforcement expert and rolled out surveillance software called “PolyGraph” built with analytics firm Chainalysis, and Kalshi for strengthening their detection protocols.

The scrutiny follows a string of cases involving alleged insider trading by public officials and government employees.

Recent findings suggest that A U.S. soldier was charged in April over alleged Polymarket trades tied to a military operation that resulted in the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Then, in August, the CFTC fined a former White House teleprompter operator for betting on presidential speeches.

The push also lands amid broader pressure on the sector, with the CFTC moving to assert authority over prediction markets in its fight against several states, while Sen. Elizabeth Warren sets her sights on the industry as the incoming Senate Banking chair.

OpenAI’s fresh payment wallet lets AI agents complete purchases using existing card networks, with plans to eventually allow preauthorized transactions.

OpenAI on Friday introduced a fresh feature allowing AI agents to make purchases on behalf of users directly within ChatGPT through existing payment networks, in collaboration with American Express, Mastercard and Visa.

Industry observers note that the wallet lets consumers authorize transactions using biometric verification, such as facial recognition or fingerprints. Payment networks generate tokenized card credentials for each approved purchase, keeping users’ actual card details from merchants and AI agents, the organization remarked.

The launch comes as AI companies seek to move beyond product recommendations into executing transactions, potentially changing how consumers interact with online merchants. OpenAI remarked it is working with payment processors and fraud prevention firms to support AI purchases through existing checkout systems.

OpenAI joins a growing field of companies developing payment systems for AI agents. Google introduced its Agent Payments Protocol in 2025, while Visa and Mastercard have introduced initiatives to support AI-initiated transactions.

It has been revealed that crypto companies are also developing payment infrastructure for AI agents. Coinbase introduced its x402 protocol in 2025, enabling autonomous stablecoin payments for digital services, while Circle launched its Agent Stack in May, allowing agents to hold and spend USDC within predefined limits. Crossmint, which provides stablecoin infrastructure, has taken a different approach, combining stablecoin wallets with traditional card networks.

Global agentic commerce transaction value is expected to reach $1.5 trillion by 2030, according to an April report from Juniper Research, up from an estimated $8 billion in 2026.

China’s $3.2 Billion AI Pipeline Still Calls for Nvidia Chips Washington Restricts.

Chinese developers are planning and building billions of dollars worth of AI data centers around Nvidia processors restricted by Washington, according to a Reuters investigation published Friday.

In a recent development, after examining more than 150 procurement notices, investment aims and corporate records, the news agency identified projects worth over 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion). Many specify Nvidia's H100, H200, or H800 chips, which provide the computing power used to train and run advanced AI models.

It has been revealed that but $3.2 billion is the total value of the projects, including buildings, electricity and other infrastructure. The documents do not establish that all the processors were obtained, or that any export laws were broken.

One proposed computing center in Fujian province is valued at 6.2 billion yuan ($873 million). Its official investment listing specifies H100 servers but is still seeking financing partners.

In Shaanxi, a state-owned engineering group won a contract linked to a 3 billion yuan center naming H100 and H200 chips. A 2.26 billion yuan project in Jilin proposes combining Nvidia hardware with Chinese processors.

Inner Mongolia has another proposed development specifying 625 H200 servers. Meanwhile, authorities in Wuxi reported that an H800 computing cluster began operating in March 2025. Operating facilities and proposed investments are not evidence of the same level of chip access.

Nvidia's processors can carry out thousands of calculations at once, making them valuable for AI training. Its widely used software also makes switching to rival systems more complicated and potentially expensive.

The United States began restricting advanced AI chip sales to China in 2022, citing national security concerns. In January 2026, the Commerce Department moved H200 export applications to case-by-case review, although sales still require licenses. H100 shipments remain more tightly restricted.

That leaves Chinese developers with a dilemma: design facilities around familiar Nvidia equipment they may struggle to acquire, or invest in alternative processors that can require software changes and additional engineering.

An IDC report cited by Reuters estimated Nvidia accounted for 34% of China's AI accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026, compared with 28% for Huawei. Those figures cover the broader chip market, not confirmed shipments of restricted models.

Chinese AI developer Z.AI has already released an image-generation model trained entirely on Huawei chips, demonstrating that competitive systems need not depend on American hardware.

Still, the newly introduced project records show how deeply Nvidia remains embedded in Chinese AI infrastructure plans. They also add pressure on U.S. officials facing congressional scrutiny over how advanced chip export rules are enforced.

#29. Strategy Sends Crucial Message on Bitcoin's Quantum Security

Strategy Sends Crucial Message on Bitcoin's Quantum Security

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Sumber: https://u.today/strategy-sends-crucial-message-on-bitcoins-quantum-security

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Strategy, the world's largest corporate Bitcoin (BTC) holder, has sent an vital message regarding Bitcoin’s future resistance to quantum computing attacks.
  • The tech giant, which was co-founded by renowned Bitcoin champion Michael Saylor, recently posted on X that the Bitcoin network can implement upcoming security measures as and when they are needed.
  • “Quantum-resistant upgrades can be adopted if & when it's needed,” wrote Strategy.

Strategy, the world's largest corporate Bitcoin (BTC) holder, has sent an vital message regarding Bitcoin’s future resistance to quantum computing attacks.

The tech giant, which was co-founded by renowned Bitcoin champion Michael Saylor, recently posted on X that the Bitcoin network can implement upcoming security measures as and when they are needed.

“Quantum-resistant upgrades can be adopted if & when it's needed,” wrote Strategy.

These comments come at a time when the crypto industry is debating whether the rise of quantum computing could, in the long run, threaten Bitcoin’s cryptographic security.

Given that Bitcoin leverages elliptic curve cryptography for transaction security, quantum computing could pose a significant threat to Bitcoin.

A sufficiently powerful quantum computer has the potential to reverse-engineer private keys from exposed public keys. This could give attackers access to the Bitcoin holdings associated with those keys.

At this point, there is no known publicly available quantum computer that can successfully break Bitcoin’s cryptography in this manner.

While speaking at the World Bank in Washington in October, Saylor remarked that the Bitcoin network would be able to defend itself against any realistic quantum computing threat by coming together and upgrading the software.

Saylor estimated that such an upgrade would take about 90 days once a worldwide consensus is reached on the need for quantum-resistant cryptography.

Saylor also warned against the hasty introduction of fresh cryptography. He reasoned that more complex security measures may themselves introduce weaknesses.

However, the 90-day estimate has come under scrutiny because such a network-wide shift would involve developers agreeing on technical changes and Bitcoin consumers moving their funds to upcoming, secure addresses.

Interestingly, Strategy has also initiated efforts aimed at research and development for Bitcoin’s long-term security.

In July, Strategy was part of a group of seven major financial institutions and crypto companies, including BlackRock and Coinbase, that formed the Bitcoin Security Consortium.

Recent findings suggest that the Bitcoin Security Consortium has committed $15 million over three years. One of the areas of focus of the consortium is post-quantum cryptography.

In fact, Bitcoin developers are already working on ways to address the quantum computing problem.

One of the most prominent proposals is Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 360 (BIP-360). This BIP introduces a newly introduced type of transaction output, Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR).

The FBI says North Korean hackers reuse stolen accounts and webcam footage to draw the next contact into a fake meeting.

North Korean hackers are using stolen webcam recordings to impersonate crypto workers in fake meetings with their contacts, turning one victim's familiar face into bait for the next attack, the FBI warns.

Industry observers note that the Justice Department announced disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used in FaceStealer on November 12. It remarked the scheme had caused more than $400 million in cryptocurrency theft over the preceding 18 months and that the FBI had seized over 900 victim webcam videos under a federal warrant.

The DOJ release treats FaceStealer separately from the Binance theft, which CryptoSlate has covered through the FBI's attribution and the exchange's asset-replenishment delays.

In a recent development, in its November 12 FLASH advisory, the FBI describes attackers taking over genuine accounts on services including Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord. Access to chat histories lets them tailor an invitation to earlier conversations, giving a upcoming approach the context of an existing relationship.

A legitimate calendaring service can handle the scheduling. The malicious meeting link arrives shortly before the call, directing the target to a copycat Zoom or Microsoft Teams session controlled by the attackers.

According to recent reports, once the target enters, stored webcam footage makes it appear that the known contact has joined. Attackers can simulate several participants. The familiar person on screen can therefore be a real prior victim's recording, rather than a live participant.

The FBI claims FaceStealer still overwhelmingly relies on stolen genuine videos. Generated deepfakes provide an additional way to impersonate participants.

The target's webcam becomes part of the attack before the supposed troubleshooting begins. The FLASH says recording starts when the target first clicks the imposter meeting link. The attackers can later use that footage to impersonate the target.

In a recent development, that is where the scheme joins theft to impersonation. Access to the computer can expose cryptocurrency or other valuable access. Stolen communication accounts, contact lists and webcam footage give the hackers material for the next approach. The FBI's FaceStealer resource page describes the same cycle of compromise, account hijacking and fake meetings.

The damage is not necessarily immediate. The FBI reported cases in which cryptocurrency theft and communication-account takeovers came months to more than a year after the initial compromise. A quiet period after a suspicious meeting therefore does not establish that a device or account is safe.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blockstream’s new custody system, developed with Thales, uses dedicated hardware for transaction signing as Adam Back advocates for offline security to reduce cyber risks.
  • Adam Back’s Bitcoin infrastructure tech giant Blockstream has released a new institutional digital asset custody solution developed with French technology group Thales, as the cryptographer pushes for simpler, offline security systems to protect Bitcoin against increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.
  • The solution, announced Friday, combines Thales’ hardware security modules (HSMs) with Blockstream’s Secure Multi-Party Computation (Secure-MPC) technology, allowing institutions to authorize transactions while keeping sensitive cryptographic operations within dedicated security hardware, according to the company.

Blockstream’s new custody system, developed with Thales, uses dedicated hardware for transaction signing as Adam Back advocates for offline security to reduce cyber risks.

Adam Back’s Bitcoin infrastructure tech giant Blockstream has released a new institutional digital asset custody solution developed with French technology group Thales, as the cryptographer pushes for simpler, offline security systems to protect Bitcoin against increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.

The solution, announced Friday, combines Thales’ hardware security modules (HSMs) with Blockstream’s Secure Multi-Party Computation (Secure-MPC) technology, allowing institutions to authorize transactions while keeping sensitive cryptographic operations within dedicated security hardware, according to the company.

Unlike conventional MPC implementations that may perform portions of the signing process outside dedicated security hardware, Blockstream stated its architecture executes the entire signing protocol within the protected environment of Thales’ HSMs.

Blockstream co-founder and CEO Adam Back, a pioneering cryptographer whose Hashcash system helped lay the groundwork for Bitcoin’s proof-of-work mechanism, told Cointelegraph that conventional MPC protocols are often too complex and require too much communication between devices to be practical for fully offline cold storage.

“When people talk about MPC, they’re talking about some very esoteric and complicated protocols that are hard to secure and are very interactive. So you can’t really use them in a cold storage setting,” Back said.

Related: Blockstream rejects ransom as Liquid hackers hold nearly 600 BTC.

Back pointed to the Binance $6.3 billion hack as an example of the risks facing internet-connected custody infrastructure, arguing that keeping signing devices offline can help prevent unauthorized access.

According to Binance’s investigation, attackers compromised employee devices and obtained credentials that allowed them to access the exchange’s wallet-signing infrastructure.

He also mentioned that AI could make existing security challenges more difficult to manage, particularly by helping attackers discover subtle flaws in complex MPC implementations.

“The AIs can help attackers find small implementation errors and things like that, which may not be obvious,” he noted.

Asked whether the broader custody industry would adopt similar offline security models, Back remarked he hoped so, arguing that institutions should “adapt to the environment” by moving assets into cold storage to reduce exposure to potential AI-assisted attacks.

“Complexity is the enemy of security. And going back to basics is the answer, you know, just cold-store it,” Back added.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that adding up the disclosures in JPMorgan’s quarterly 13F, the form large institutional managers must file with the Securities and Exchange Commission to report their holdings, the bank held roughly $981 million across spot Bitcoin ETFs, Michael Saylor’s Strategy, and crypto exchange Coinbase as of Sept.

JPMorgan’s Bitcoin and Crypto-Linked Holdings Approach $1 Billion.

JPMorgan Chase, whose CEO has spent years deriding crypto, is now sitting on close to $1 billion worth of crypto-linked stocks and funds, a regulatory filing demonstrates, after the bank deepened those positions in the third quarter.

It has been revealed that adding up the disclosures in JPMorgan’s quarterly 13F, the form large institutional managers must file with the Securities and Exchange Commission to report their holdings, the bank held roughly $981 million across spot Bitcoin ETFs, Michael Saylor’s Strategy, and crypto exchange Coinbase as of Sept. 30.

Counting its stakes in Robinhood and Bitcoin miners, the total likely tips past $1 billion.

Sources indicate that the largest piece is BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, or IBIT, where JPMorgan reported 11,408,930 shares worth about $540 million, a 9.6% increase in shares from the prior quarter, when the holding was valued at roughly $356 million. It held smaller positions in Grayscale’s and Bitwise’s Bitcoin ETFs, bringing its total spot Bitcoin ETF exposure to around $549 million.

The bank also leaned further into Strategy, the Bitcoin treasury firm, raising its stake 36% to 848,932 shares, up from 624,387 at the end of June. That position was valued at about $131.3 million, up from $57.9 million a quarter earlier, reflecting both the added shares and a rise in Strategy’s stock over the period.

A roughly $301 million stake in Coinbase rounds out the core holdings, alongside positions in Robinhood and miners including Core Scientific and Hut 8. JPMorgan also disclosed sizable options tied to both IBIT and Strategy.

The company’s 13F is a snapshot as of Sept. 30 and doesn’t capture moves since, nor does it necessarily reflect directional bets. Banks often hold such positions to hedge or to facilitate client trades rather than to wager on price, so the near-$1 billion figure is better read as the scale of JPMorgan’s crypto-market activity than as a conviction call.

That nuance matters given CEO Jamie Dimon, who has called Bitcoin worthless and likened crypto to a fraud, even as the bank he runs steadily builds out digital-asset services.

Sources indicate that those services have expanded quickly. JPMorgan recently issued its first price forecast for Bitcoin, rolled out a deposit token called JPM Coin tied to bank dollars on Ethereum, and explored tokenized stocks alongside BlackRock and the DTCC.

Sources indicate that the disclosure also lands during a rough stretch for Bitcoin funds. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have bled more than $1.4 billion over a recent five-day span as investors cut risk, a reminder that the institutional appetite captured in JPMorgan’s September snapshot has cooled since.

Bitcoin, which traded near $155 per Strategy share levels at quarter-end, has since slid well off its highs, today trading below $69,000.

According to recent reports, aave lenders supplying DAI on Polygon could see their share of borrower interest fall from 75% to 30% under a November 12 proposal by TokenLogic. The proposal would redirect more interest to Aave’s DAO treasury, with uneven cuts to lender returns across its markets.

In a recent development, the November 12 proposal covers 54 reserves across 12 Aave V3 instances and Ethereum V2. TokenLogic estimates about $4 million in additional annualized DAO revenue using November 9 balances and rates. That total includes roughly $1 million from Plasma USDT0, a change that would enter the formal proposal only once its terms are finalized.

According to recent reports, in Aave’s lending system, the mechanism is the reserve factor: the portion of borrower interest allocated to the DAO instead of suppliers. Raising it changes who receives the interest, without directly changing the borrowing-rate curve. TokenLogic argues the larger share would better compensate the DAO for the risks attached to borrowable reserves.

Polygon V3 DAI illustrates how much that allocation can matter. TokenLogic proposes raising its reserve factor from 25% to 70%, with a modeled supply APY reduction of 270 basis points, or 2.70 percentage points. The same line projects $94,373 in additional annual DAO revenue.

Recent findings suggest that with the amount of borrower interest unchanged, suppliers’ share would fall from 75% to 30%. The treasury would receive the difference. In that fixed-input model, the revenue gain comes from a smaller payment to lenders, without requiring more borrowing or a higher price for the same loan.

Polygon DAI illustrates TokenLogic’s November 12 proposal: the interest allocation changes while the model holds borrowing and rates fixed.

The proposed 70% reserve factor leaves suppliers 30% of borrower interest, down from 75%.

The cooperative noted that these figures put the industry ahead of the G20’s target for one-hour end-to-end processing by 2027 in the interbank leg of the journey.

The same report emphasizes that the “last mile”, the period after a payment reaches the receiving bank and before it is credited to the beneficiary’s account, still accounts for about 80% of the average end-to-end journey time.

Across 40 receiving markets analyzed, median last-mile processing sat near one hour in roughly one-third of cases, with wide variation between cross-border markets.

The conglomerate has called for greater use of one-leg-out models that connect international payments to domestic instant systems to reduce those final delays.

According to recent reports, digital Asset Investor’s reply to the Swift post was brief: “I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP.” The comment references the XRP Ledger’s typical ledger close time of roughly 3-5 seconds, which provides finality for on-ledger transfers.

In Ripple’s On-Demand Liquidity (ODL) model, XRP is used as a bridge asset so that currency conversion and settlement can occur without pre-funded nostro accounts.

End-to-end ODL flows that include exchange conversions have been described in the 3-5 second range for the core ledger step, though real-world completion including compliance and local payouts is often measured in seconds to a few minutes depending on the corridor.

The two claims are not measuring identical segments of a payment. Swift’s 40-second figure tracks time to the recipient institution, while the longer last-mile delays occur after that point.

Over the same period, the market cap of tokenized funds on Solana, Ethereum and zkSync Era increased by $29 million, $10.8 million and $3.5 million, respectively.

According to recent reports, stellar is currently the second-largest blockchain for tokenized funds after Ethereum, according to Token Terminal. In this context, the compliance tools are built into the base layer of the network, and an issuer can vet investors through trustlines, freeze accounts and claw back assets.

Recent findings suggest that transactions on Stellar settle in 3 to 5 seconds, and the fees on the network are measured in fractions of a cent. Besides, customers can move funds to and from fiat currencies through local providers, which are called anchors on Stellar.

It has been revealed that franklin Templeton's BENJI money market fund has run on Stellar since 2021, and it was the first U.S. mutual fund on a public blockchain.

Today, Spiko, Ondo and WisdomTree are also building their own funds and tokenized U.S. Treasuries on Stellar. Spiko offers euro funds managed by Amundi, and Ondo has debuted its USDY token on the network.

It has been revealed that in May 2026, DTCC and the Stellar Development Foundation declared that the Depository Trust Company (DTC) will tokenize the assets it holds in custody on Stellar. According to DTCC, DTC-tokenized assets are expected to become available on the network in the first half of 2027.

On Nov. 12, DTCC also declared that it will connect its tokenization service to Solana in the second half of 2027.

Payward’s adjusted EBITDA fell 66% year over year to $60 million, even as its share of global spot trading nearly doubled and fee-based services expanded.

Kraken’s parent tech giant Payward nearly doubled its share of global crypto spot trading to 6.5% in September from 3.3% a year earlier, even as weaker trading activity weighed on its earnings.

Industry observers note that the market-share gain means Payward captured a larger portion of spot trading relative to competitors, rather than an increase in trading activity across its platforms. The company handled $353 billion in transactions in the third quarter, down 30% from a year earlier, according to financial results released Friday.

According to recent reports, the two figures measure different things. The market share tracks its portion of global spot trading across its platforms in September, compared with a year earlier, while Payward’s quarterly transaction volume includes activity across multiple products, including spot, margin, equities, payments and certain derivatives.

It has been revealed that adjusted EBITDA fell to $60 million from the $178.6 million reported a year earlier. Total platform margin fell 12% to $487 million. Payward introduced that measure this quarter to replace adjusted revenue, adding a deduction for staking rewards paid to customers.

Payward has spent the past two years expanding beyond its core cryptocurrency exchange business through acquisitions in derivatives, proprietary trading, tokenized assets and payments. The strategy aims to diversify revenue beyond transaction fees, which fluctuate with market activity.

Industry observers note that its purchases include futures broker NinjaTrader and proprietary trading firm Breakout in 2025, followed by the acquisition of US-regulated derivatives platform Bitnomial in May 2026. The tech giant also expanded into stablecoin payments with its purchase of Reap in July.

According to recent reports, those businesses contributed to a broader mix of trading and service-based activity in the third quarter. The number of derivatives contracts on which Payward charges a per-contract fee rose 84% to 66 million. Margin from subscriptions, trader evaluations and other paid services rose 59% to $125 million.

Industry observers note that breakout, which charges traders for evaluations that can qualify them for funded trading accounts, was included for the full quarter after joining in September 2025. The July purchase of Reap added a stablecoin payments and card-issuing business. The organization did not quantify either acquisition’s contribution to the quarter.

Related: Kraken parent Payward acquires Magic Labs’ wallet business.

In a recent development, results improved from the second quarter despite remaining below year-earlier levels. Total transaction volume rose 22%, while total platform margin increased 12% to $487 million from $436 million.

It has been revealed that the improvement was not driven by trading alone. Margin earned from assets customers hold on Payward’s platforms, including staking-related services, rose 26% to $128 million. That accounted for roughly half of the $51 million quarterly increase in total platform margin.

Adjusted EBITDA climbed to $60 million from $23 million, while its margin relative to total platform margin rose to 12% from 5%. Compared with a year earlier, however, adjusted EBITDA was down 66%, underscoring the pressure on profitability despite a growing contribution from services less directly tied to trading activity. Asset- and access-based services accounted for 52% of total platform margin, up from 46% a year earlier.

In a recent development, that shift could matter for an eventual public listing. Payward confidentially filed for a US IPO in November 2025 but paused its plans in March as market conditions weakened. By September, the earliest potential listing window under consideration was the second quarter of 2027.

#62. Dormant Bitcoin Wallets Wake Up After 16 Years, Moving $6.9 Million

Dormant Bitcoin Wallets Wake Up After 16 Years, Moving $6.9 Million

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://decrypt.co/383264/dormant-bitcoin-wallets-wake-up-after-16-years

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dormant Bitcoin Wallets Wake Up After 16 Years, Moving $6.9 Million.
  • Two Bitcoin addresses that had been dormant since 2010 suddenly moved $6.9 million worth of BTC on Friday, bringing two early mining rewards back into circulation after more than 16 years.
  • Blockchain tracking service Whale Alert flagged the first transfer at 4:08 a.m.

Dormant Bitcoin Wallets Wake Up After 16 Years, Moving $6.9 Million.

Two Bitcoin addresses that had been dormant since 2010 suddenly moved $6.9 million worth of BTC on Friday, bringing two early mining rewards back into circulation after more than 16 years.

Blockchain tracking service Whale Alert flagged the first transfer at 4:08 a.m. UTC on November 13, when 50 BTC worth approximately $3.44 million moved from an address that had not spent its original mining reward since September 2010.

Just over two minutes later, another 50 BTC moved from a separate wallet with an equally long history.

Sources indicate that both transfers involved Bitcoin originally generated through mining, rather than coins purchased on an exchange. Their combined value today was approximately $6,885,068.

The coins came from two blocks mined on September 8 and September 19, 2010, respectively. Back then, Bitcoin traded for roughly six cents, meaning each 50 BTC reward was worth about three bucks.

At Friday's transaction prices of around $68,800 per Bitcoin, their combined value had increased approximately 1,147,511 times, equivalent to a 114,751,033% increase.

It has been revealed that that percentage measures the appreciation in Bitcoin's market price (what’s known as unrealized gains), not money the holder has actually made by selling (which would be known as realized gains). In fact, it’s unknown whether this was a peer-to-peer transaction, an OTC sell, or simply a wallet switch for security reasons.

According to recent reports, the $3 valuation is also an estimate. Bitcoin barely had a functioning market in September 2010, with historical prices showing a trading range of around five to seven cents. The Mt. Gox exchange had only opened that July, with its first recorded trade taking place at $0.04951 per coin.

The transfers are part of a broader trend of ancient Bitcoin wallets waking up in 2026. According to Galaxy Research data highlighted in August, Bitcoin that had remained untouched for at least a decade was moving at a pace rarely seen in previous years. In one 10-day stretch alone, six wallets dating back to 2011, 2012, and 2014 transferred a combined 553.59 BTC, worth more than $40 million at the time.

It has been revealed that some of those movements have been linked to security concerns, wallet upgrades, or transfers to professional custodians rather than outright selling. Friday's activity adds another 100 BTC to the growing list of early Bitcoin holdings changing hands—or at least changing addresses—after more than a decade of silence.

The blockchain provides a detailed record of where the money moved, but it doesn't reveal who controls the receiving wallets.

The first transaction split the 50 BTC into two latest addresses, sending nearly 49.99 BTC to one and approximately 0.01 BTC to another, minus a tiny network fee.

The second transaction followed a similar pattern, transferring nearly 49 BTC to one address and approximately 1 BTC to another.

It has been revealed that both transactions cost just 1,110 satoshis each in network fees, equivalent to approximately $0.75. A satoshi is Bitcoin's smallest unit, worth one hundred-millionth of a BTC.

As of an on-chain check at approximately 14:00 UTC Friday, the 100 BTC had not moved again from their fresh destinations following the consolidation, and no sale has been identified.

💡 Key Takeaways

Sources indicate that human engineers designed the guardrails and release checks. Application security still needs testing on the real cloud.

Amazon released AWS Emulator on Nov. 11, a local tool that imitates AWS services so developers can test cloud applications on their own machines. The firm says autonomous AI agents wrote and reviewed its implementation.

In a recent development, in Amazon's engineering account, engineer Matthew Goldberg indicates his team neither wrote nor reviewed the emulator code. He also describes the substantial engineering work needed to turn an experiment into a product, including the guardrails and checks that determine which changes can ship.

According to recent reports, amazon describes three teams of agents: one manages fidelity tests, another finds differences between the emulator and real AWS, and a third fixes individual challenges. Changes face checks for compilation, coding standards, security and regressions before merging, according to the firm.

In a recent development, the test agents work from public AWS API models and verify their scenarios against the real cloud. The public evaluation suite indicates every fidelity test was checked against at least two sandboxed AWS accounts.

AWS calls the degree of agreement with its cloud services “fidelity.” A test passes when the emulator matches AWS for every call in that workflow, including status codes, resulting resources, side effects and errors, according to its fidelity documentation. Returning success where AWS returns an error fails that test.

The boundary is coverage. The evaluation repository explicitly says behavior without a fidelity test is unverified. Passing a scenario establishes a match for that scenario; it does not establish that every way an application uses AWS will work.

In a recent development, thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

AWS defines a pass within a tested workflow. Untested behavior and application security sit beyond that conclusion.

A passing workflow is evidence for that scenario. It does not validate all AWS behavior or application security.

Diagram shows AWS's pass rule, not a particular test result or measured coverage. Application security still requires testing on real AWS before production.

Industry observers note that qualitative diagram of AWS's published fidelity definition and testing limits. Branches compare the real-AWS reference with emulator replay; they do not represent simultaneous live tests, amounts or coverage proportions.

Recent findings suggest that diagram highlights AWS's pass rule, not a particular test result or measured coverage. Application security still requires testing on real AWS before production.

Security has a separate limit. AWS's security guidance warns against using the emulator to determine whether an application is secure. It does not check AWS KMS key policies or Amazon S3 bucket policies, and a request denied by AWS may succeed locally.

Agent review of implementation security therefore cannot be read as validation of a user's application permissions. The emulator is for building and testing, not production workloads. AWS instructs developers to test their whole application and security settings on real AWS before production.

For builders adopting agent-written software, the release makes the acceptance process as relevant as the code's authorship: which behaviors are checked, what remains outside coverage, and where the developer must still test against the real service.

Coinbase’s trust organization received final clearance as lawmakers seek records on crypto firms’ compliance and potential conflicts of interest.

Sources indicate that federal regulators are opening more avenues for crypto companies to operate under US rules, while congressional investigators are asking to see the records behind those decisions. Lawmakers want to know how regulators justified new trust charters, how crypto companies handled compliance and what dealings they had with people tied to President Donald Trump’s administration.

On Nov. 9, Coinbase announced that its national trust company had received final approval to open. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted preliminary conditional approval in April. The company stated the charter gives its custody business a consistent federal framework.

Recent findings suggest that lawmakers had been questioning how federal regulators were using their existing authority to expand crypto companies’ reach. In a May 18 letter to the OCC, Sen. Elizabeth Warren challenged at least nine crypto trust-charter approvals, including Coinbase’s earlier conditional approval. She asked for the applications, the legal analyses behind the approvals and any related communications between OCC officials and the White House or Trump family.

According to recent reports, four days before Coinbase’s announcement, Sen. Richard Blumenthal renewed demands for records from Binance, Tether and two Trump-linked ventures. He gave them until Jan. 4, 2027, to turn over the requested records voluntarily and warned that his subcommittee could take other steps to obtain them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fed Chair Warsh Wants Answers on AI Inflation—and Bitcoin May Feel the Impact.
  • Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will convene a public forum Monday to examine whether artificial intelligence will bring down inflation, drive prices higher, or replace American workers.
  • The November 16 conference in San Francisco will bring together technology executives, economists, and employers to examine how AI is reshaping the economy.

Fed Chair Warsh Wants Answers on AI Inflation—and Bitcoin May Feel the Impact.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will convene a public forum Monday to examine whether artificial intelligence will bring down inflation, drive prices higher, or replace American workers.

The November 16 conference in San Francisco will bring together technology executives, economists, and employers to examine how AI is reshaping the economy.

The findings could influence how the Fed approaches interest rates, a major factor in Bitcoin's price movements as investors weigh whether to put money into risky assets or safer alternatives.

Warsh has argued that AI could help companies produce more goods and services at lower costs, easing inflation without requiring the Fed to keep borrowing expensive.

But some of his colleagues see a different problem: The AI boom is already making things more expensive, while the promised productivity benefits remain largely theoretical.

Building data centers requires enormous quantities of electricity, computer chips, construction materials, and skilled workers. When technology companies compete for those limited resources, prices rise.

Fed Governor Lisa Cook warned in September that AI investment was adding inflationary pressure and delaying the central bank's return to its 2% inflation target.

If AI eventually allows businesses to produce more without raising costs, inflation could cool, giving policymakers room to lower interest rates.

Lower rates generally make risky assets like Bitcoin or tech stocks more attractive because government bonds and savings accounts offer smaller returns, encouraging investors to seek higher gains elsewhere.

But if AI spending keeps inflation elevated, the Fed could maintain high interest rates or raise them further. That would make borrowing more expensive, strengthen the appeal of interest-bearing assets, and potentially drain money from speculative investments, including cryptocurrencies.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin is already feeling that pressure. The cryptocurrency dropped below $69,000 Friday as stronger-than-expected inflation figures fueled concerns about another Fed rate hike.

AI also has a more direct connection to the Bitcoin industry than most may think of.

Industry observers note that both AI data centers and Bitcoin mining operations need access to large amounts of electricity. As AI companies compete for power and infrastructure, miners face pressure to secure affordable energy or consider more profitable alternatives.

Some are already abandoning Bitcoin mining altogether. Hyperscale Data shut down mining operations at its Michigan facility in September to accommodate an AI customer under a deal potentially worth more than $1.2 billion. The same has happened with other big names like Coreweave and other former Ethereum miners from its proof-of-work era.

Meanwhile, AI's potential impact on employment adds another complication.

Fed Governor Michael Barr warned Thursday of possible “serious short-term disruptions” as businesses increasingly replace human tasks with AI systems.

Widespread job losses could weaken consumer spending, slow economic growth, and eventually increase pressure on the Fed to cut rates. But a deteriorating economy could also push investors away from Bitcoin as they look to reduce risk.

Warsh himself acknowledged in August that AI represents “a newly introduced variable” for monetary policy.

The question now is whether AI's economic benefits will arrive quickly enough to outweigh the costs of building it.

It has been revealed that monday's conference will not determine the Fed's next interest-rate decision, scheduled for December 9. But it could offer clues about how policymakers view a technology boom that is increasingly influencing both Wall Street and the crypto market.

He’s calling on investors to remain calm amid another significant drop for the world's largest cryptocurrency.

On X, Lunde recently shared some technical indicators suggesting the possibility of a major Bitcoin turnaround after weeks of massive selling.

“This is a great place to buy BTC,” Lunde said.

Among the indicators Lunde considers is the fact that BTC has returned to its 200-week moving average (MA). This is a long-term technical indicator widely tracked by crypto traders. It’s used to identify potential market bottoms.

According to Lunde, the daily Relative Strength Index (RSI) for Bitcoin has fallen to 25, which indicates that the market has become oversold.

Whenever the RSI goes below 30, it suggests that the asset has been oversold, experiencing heavy selling pressure. It doesn’t necessarily mean that the price will reverse higher.

Lunde also noted that Bitcoin has experienced the fifth-largest wave of exchange-traded fund (ETF) outflows on record. There’s also been a large reduction in leverage on Bitcoin ETFs.

According to recent reports, exposure to 2x leveraged ETFs has now reached a level not seen in the last 2.5 years. That’s a massive reduction in leverage on the asset. “So, speculative stuff is off,” Lunde said.

“Don’t press the red panic button!” Lunde added.

Bitcoin sales, valuation losses and rising borrowing costs weighed on the Japanese company’s earnings despite higher revenue and operating profit.

Metaplanet swung to a $170 million net loss in the first nine months of 2026, hit by a decline in the value of its Bitcoin holdings and a loss on the sale of 10,000 coins to demonstrate its ability to raise cash.

According to recent reports, the Japanese tech giant, the world’s second-largest publicly traded corporate Bitcoin (BTC) holder, posted a net loss of 27.16 billion yen (about $170 million), compared with a profit of 13.53 billion yen ($84.6 million) in the same period last year. A 19.17 billion yen ($119.8 million) loss on the Bitcoin sale and an 8.04 billion yen ($50.3 million) loss from a decline in the value of its Bitcoin holdings outweighed gains in the operating business.

Sources indicate that over the quarter, Metaplanet sold the 10,000 BTC for 124.7 billion yen and temporarily held the proceeds in cash, stablecoins and other liquid assets. It then spent 149.9 billion yen to buy 11,000 BTC, paying 9.3% more per coin on average. The company said the sale was meant to show rating agencies and bond investors that it could turn its Bitcoin into cash to meet financing obligations. At the end of September, holdings rose by a net 1,000 coins to 44,000 BTC.

According to recent reports, top 10 largest Bitcoin treasury companies. Source: BitcoinTreasuries.NET.

Metaplanet borrowed against its Bitcoin holdings during the quarter, increasing the amount it owed under the credit line to $649.5 million at the end of September from $414 million at the end of June.

The company remarked it funded Bitcoin purchases from the second quarter onward with money borrowed under the credit line, proceeds from bond sales and the exercise of stock acquisition rights, and revenue from its Bitcoin options business.

Metaplanet’s interest expense rose 56% from the previous quarter to 1.36 billion yen ($8.5 million). Short-term borrowings and bonds payable totaled 110.5 billion yen ($691 million) at the end of September.

Recent findings suggest that for the nine months through September, revenue rose 30.5% to 5.9 billion yen ($36.9 million), while operating profit increased 26.5% to 3.48 billion yen ($21.8 million). The manufacturer cut its full-year revenue forecast to 6.5 billion yen ($40.6 million) from 16 billion yen ($100 million).

Metaplanet’s earnings come as Bitcoin treasury companies face mounting pressure from incoming stock index removals and falling Bitcoin prices.

Industry observers note that index provider MSCI confirmed Wednesday that Strategy, Metaplanet and Upexi would be removed from its equity indexes at the Nov. 30 market close, potentially prompting funds that track those benchmarks to sell the shares. JPMorgan previously estimated that Strategy’s removal could result in roughly $2.8 billion in selling pressure from MSCI-linked funds.

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday and was trading around $68,600 as of 4:51 p.m. UTC, down about 9% over the previous week, according to CoinGecko data.

Industry observers note that this snapshot combines Nov. 5 vault sizes and first-period Firelight limits with DAO positions referenced to its Sept. 30 quarterly reporting. The dollar estimates come from Lido’s November illustration and should not be treated as Nov. 13 balances.

Recent findings suggest that lido says ordinary price moves and liquidations using accurate prices are excluded, alongside stolen keys, user error, offchain challenges and flaws known before a protection period began. Protected markets and limits remain fixed for each 30-day period. Capital moved into a new market midway through a period becomes protected only when a later period includes it.

An independent consortium of five security and risk firms must approve Firelight’s loss assessment. Approved payments draw first on its reserve, then on staked capital.

According to recent reports, lido noted on Nov. 5 that Current Meta Treasury pays for this protection, so the premium does not come out of vault returns. That funding is separate from the DAO’s invested loss-absorbing position.

Industry observers note that the DAO layer operates under its own mandate and is not restricted to specific causes. Once a loss of at least 1% of a vault’s TVL is confirmed, the Growth Committee can burn up to all DAO-held shares in that affected vault. The mandate can be changed by DAO vote.

Lido’s original DAO mechanism was backed by an allocation of $3 million worth of wstETH to EarnETH and $2 million in USDC to EarnUSD. Those deposits hold shares on ordinary depositor terms, earning returns and carrying risk. Burning them reduces the share supply to offset losses for other holders. The capital available through this mechanism is limited to the DAO’s vault position.

Industry observers note that both layers operate at vault level, so depositors do not need to submit individual compensation requests. Incident approval, the DAO’s activation threshold and each layer’s capital limits still apply. Lido also states neither layer is insurance or a guarantee, and that Firelight protection gives depositors no right of action against a Firelight party.

A loss outside Firelight’s scope may still qualify under the DAO’s separate mandate. Any loss left after applicable protection, including amounts above market limits or beyond available capital and DAO shares, can remain with depositors.

FutureBit is putting its Apollo III Full Node on sale Friday at four Micro Center stores, the first time customers can walk into a shop and take home one of the Brooklyn organization’s bitcoin miners.

Industry observers note that the compact home miner, which also runs a full bitcoin node, will be sold in Brooklyn, Miami, Tustin, California, and Austin, Texas, as those stores open Friday, FutureBit stated in a release. The four-store launch coincides with the grand opening of Micro Center’s fresh Austin store, the chain’s 31st U.S. location and its third in Texas.

In a recent development, customers will also be able to reserve a unit online for in-store pickup, the company stated. It did not say how many units each store has in stock, or what Micro Center is charging for them.

Until now, buyers in North America had to order the machine from FutureBit’s website, where the company indicates units are in stock and ship in two to three days. Putting it on a computer-store shelf lets a customer look at the hardware, ask how it works and carry it out the same day.

Industry observers note that “When we started FutureBit, we made weekly trips to the DIY electronics section at the Brooklyn Micro Center to buy parts,” stated John Stefanopoulos, founder of FutureBit. “On Friday, someone can walk into that same store, ask how Bitcoin mining works and take home a miner we designed just down the street. We couldn’t be more excited to work with Micro Center on our first physical store launch.”.

In a recent development, futureBit’s own shop lists the Apollo III Full Node at $1,099.99 without a storage drive, $1,299.99 with 1 terabyte of SSD storage and $1,399.99 with 2 terabytes. A cheaper, miner-only “Standard” model starts at $899.99 but does not include the full node.

The Full Node is rated at up to 18 terahashes per second in Turbo mode, at about 325 watts. In Eco mode, it is listed at about 12 TH/s and 150 watts, with noise under 35 decibels. A Super Eco mode is listed at about 8 TH/s and 80 watts. Power can be adjusted from 50 to 400 watts, and Turbo mode is much louder, at about 55 decibels. Those power figures are measured at the board and can vary by 10%, the product page claims.

In a recent development, the unit is a 6.5-by-6.5-by-6-inch cube that weighs 6.5 pounds, comes with a one-year limited warranty and is assembled in the United States. It uses latest 3-nanometer, American-designed chips, a custom controller and 8 GB of memory, and it includes a built-in solo mining pool. Buyers can also point the miner at a standard bitcoin mining pool. FutureBit claims the full node and solo-mining features require an SSD, which is not included in the $1,099.99 configuration.

According to recent reports, bitcoin Magazine covered the Apollo III’s debut in February, when FutureBit introduced the hardware as a way for individuals to run both a miner and a node at home. The point, the tech giant has long argued, is not to compete with industrial mines on cost.

A single Apollo III at 18 TH/s is a sliver of the bitcoin network. A home-scale setup in that range still faces expected times to a solo block measured in centuries at recent difficulty, Bitcoin Magazine previously noted. Even so, a miner running through FutureBit’s Apollo Solo setup found block 973,262 on Oct. 26 and collected the full 3.154 bitcoin reward.

Recent findings suggest that futureBit, based in Brooklyn, has built consumer mining hardware since 2015. Stefanopoulos has framed store shelves as a way to put more hash rate and more nodes in living rooms. The manufacturer did not say whether the Micro Center test will expand beyond the four stores that began selling the Apollo III on Friday.

Both readings were 0.1 percentage points below market expectations but the annual increase was the largest since November 2022.

In a recent development, “Leading the October advance in final demand prices, the index for final demand goods increased 0.5 percent. Prices for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent,” the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported Friday.

In a recent development, US PPI one-month percentage change. Source: BLS.

Fed target-rate probability comparison for the December FOMC meeting. Source: CME Group.

“If high inflation is about the Strait of Hormuz and oil, 75 basis points won’t do anything about that. If the issue is that the pace of underlying inflation has risen, then 75 basis points is much too timid to get this under control,” he wrote.

Home » Trendsetter News » XRP Exchange Balances Hit Yearly High, but Long-Term Holders Stay Put.

XRP exchange balances have reached a one-year high, while the share of tokens untouched for over a year nears its annual peak.

XRP held on exchanges has reached a one-year high even as the share of coins untouched for more than a year approaches its own annual peak, according to figures cited by wealth-focused commentator Kamilah Stevenson.

Her latest video examines that split following a roughly 10% price decline, arguing that investors’ financial circumstances can matter as much as their market convictions.

Sources indicate that stevenson cites CryptoQuant data showing approximately 11.8 billion XRP on exchanges, the highest balance in a year. That puts more tokens within easy reach of trading, although exchange deposits alone do not establish that holders intend to sell.

Meanwhile, Glassnode figures cited in the video put the share of XRP unmoved for more than a year at roughly 56%, up from 51% in January. Stevenson also claims XRP exchange-traded funds still hold about 1.19 billion tokens, despite a small outflow ending a reported 13-week inflow streak.

“Both groups saw the same price,” she notes. “They reacted to it in completely opposite ways.”.

The contrast is striking, but the metrics have limits. Coins remaining stationary demonstrate inactivity, not necessarily fresh buying or confidence, and neither measure establishes where XRP’s price goes next.

Dr. Stevenson identifies three recurring sources of selling pressure: leverage, investing money needed for near-term expenses, and entering a volatile market without a plan.

She cites roughly $25.7 million in XRP liquidations on Binance during a recent sell-off as an example of positions being closed regardless of investors’ intentions.

Her broader bullish case rests partly on institutional activity involving Ripple and its RLUSD stablecoin.

The YouTube video names Standard Chartered, Cross River Bank and DriveWealth among firms involved in custody, banking or settlement developments.

Recent findings suggest that those developments should not be treated as equivalent to demand for XRP itself. Nor does institutional infrastructure guarantee that token prices will recover.

The most durable point is about liquidity: cash reserves and manageable exposure reduce the likelihood that an unexpected bill or margin call dictates a sale.

Exchange balances may signal potential selling pressure across the market; they cannot reveal which holders can afford to wait.

#88. Industry News: Trump’s First Democratic Picks for SEC and CFTC Could Reshape Crypto’s Regulators

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words)

Industry News: Trump’s First Democratic Picks for SEC and CFTC Could Reshape Crypto’s Regulators

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://decrypt.co/383260/trump-first-democratic-picks-sec-cftc-could-reshape-crypto

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trump’s First Democratic Picks for SEC and CFTC Could Reshape Crypto’s Regulators.
  • President Donald Trump has nominated four people to fill vacant seats at the two federal agencies writing the rules for crypto, in a bipartisan slate that could reshape the commissions that have increasingly taken the lead on digital-asset policy after Congress stalled.
  • The White House said Thursday it sent the nominations to the Senate: Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and Kristin Johnson and Steven Levine for the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Trump’s First Democratic Picks for SEC and CFTC Could Reshape Crypto’s Regulators.

President Donald Trump has nominated four people to fill vacant seats at the two federal agencies writing the rules for crypto, in a bipartisan slate that could reshape the commissions that have increasingly taken the lead on digital-asset policy after Congress stalled.

The White House said Thursday it sent the nominations to the Senate: Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and Kristin Johnson and Steven Levine for the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Industry observers note that each requires Senate confirmation. Notably, the slate pairs a Republican and a Democrat at each agency, with Anonick and Levine the Republicans and Rowland and Johnson the Democrats, marking the first time the administration has put forward Democratic nominees for either commission.

In a recent development, the appointments matter because of how depleted both agencies have become. The CFTC in particular has been running on a skeleton crew, operating with Michael Selig as its lone Senate-confirmed member after a wave of departures, even as it has pursued one of the most aggressive crypto agendas in its history.

Filling those seats would give the commissions the quorum and staying power to turn proposals into durable rules.

Industry observers note that both CFTC nominees come from the Senate Agriculture Committee, which shares jurisdiction over crypto market structure and will vet their nominations. Anonick, a Republican, is legislative counsel to committee Chairman John Boozman and was a lead negotiator on the panel’s portion of the Clarity Act, the crypto market-structure bill that collapsed in the Senate this fall.

It has been revealed that rowland, a Democrat, is a career CFTC attorney detailed to the committee who also worked on the Clarity Act and an earlier 2024 crypto bill. His enforcement-heavy background and party lean could introduce a dissenting voice to a commission that, under Selig, has leaned firmly pro-industry.

On the SEC side, which the Senate Banking Committee will review, the picks would replace two commissioners central to crypto policy in opposite ways. Levine, a Republican, is slated to fill the seat of Hester Peirce, the agency’s most prominent crypto advocate and the head of its Crypto Task Force.

Levine’s own views on digital assets are not well established publicly, making his future votes a key variable for whether the SEC’s crypto-friendly push holds.

Johnson, a Democrat and former CFTC commissioner, would take the seat of frequent crypto skeptic Caroline Crenshaw; at the CFTC she focused on digital-asset custody and DeFi and pressed for stronger customer protections and conflict-of-interest rules.

The timing underscores a shift following the collapse of the Clarity Act, the crypto industry’s marquee market structure bill that would have established more-favorable-than-not rules for most of crypto.

Recent findings suggest that after the legislation failed to advance in the Senate, the SEC and CFTC moved to fill the vacuum with their own authority, leaving the industry to get its “clarity” from regulators rather than legislators. A fully staffed pair of commissions would cement that dynamic.

Those agency efforts have been sweeping: The CFTC has cleared perpetual futures on individual stocks, floated bringing crypto exchanges under federal oversight, and moved to define event contracts as “swaps.” The SEC, meanwhile, rolled out an “innovation exemption” for tokenized stocks, proposed rules letting investment advisers custody crypto, and issued guidance suggesting most crypto assets aren’t securities.

Sources indicate that the nominations are the first Trump has sent for these seats in roughly a year, a gap that reflected turbulence around crypto appointments. The administration previously pulled its CFTC chair nominee, Brian Quintenz, amid a clash involving the Winklevoss twins.

The confirmation window is now tight: with the Senate heading toward Democratic control in January, Republicans have only a short lame-duck stretch to move the slate before the calculus changes.

Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has proposed a set of new rules to regulate stablecoin transactions conducted through licensed digital asset operators.

Unveiled on 12th November, the draft notification aims to prevent cryptocurrencies and stablecoins from being used for money laundering, cybercrime, and bypassing regulations governing international money transfers.

Here, it’s worth noting that this patch came soon after September’s public consultation. During the same, the regulator collected feedback from industry participants.

In a recent development, as it stands, the SEC has incorporated those changes into the latest draft. It is now seeking further public comments until 26th November.

In this, one of the key proposals is to introduce a daily transfer limit of 5 million Thai baht per customer at each regulated digital asset operator. That remarked, the limit would apply separately to incoming and outgoing stablecoin transfers. However, the value of these transactions must also be consistent with the customer’s declared income and financial position.

However, it’s notable to note that transfers between a customer’s own accounts at two SEC-supervised operators would be exempt from the limit, provided both operators follow the Travel Rule.

Simultaneously, the SEC also wants to strengthen wallet ownership verification. In this, the SEC has enabled customers to deposit stablecoins from their own verified wallets and withdraw them to wallets registered in their names.

Additionally, operators would also need to follow the Travel Rule, analyze customers, identify suspicious accounts, and track transactions connected to high-risk wallets.

These requirements would be done in order to make it harder for criminals to move illicit funds through regulated platforms.

Finally, the proposal also introduces stricter responsibilities for exchanges and brokers. Exchanges would have to publicly disclose their market makers and the digital assets for which they provide liquidity. Meanwhile, brokers would be prohibited from using liquidity providers for stablecoin-to-Thai baht trading pairs.

It has been revealed that besides that, brokers and dealers offering off-platform transactions would face a minimum transaction threshold of 3 million baht and would have to publish trading prices for transparency. Brokers would no longer be allowed to arrange off-platform trades directly between customers.

Taken together, these steps would help the SEC combat crimes that are concerning the stablecoin ecosystem in Thailand.
